claim: The rodent and primate clades diverged approximately 85 million years ago.
source: The rodent and primate clades diverged approximately 85 mya (Yang et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2004.

claim: Myelin purified from human white matter was subjected to quantitative proteomics using MSE mode and identified 332 proteins with a false discovery rate of <1%.
source: When assessing myelin by MSE, we quantified 332 proteins (Figure 1—source data 1; labeled in green in Figure 1a) with a false discovery rate (FDR) of <1% and an average sequence coverage of 39.6%.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Myelin purified from human white matter was subjected to quantitative proteomics using UDMSE mode and identified 835 proteins.
source: When using the ultra-definition (UD)MSE mode, in which ion mobility spectrometry enables an additional separation of peptides after chromatography and before mass measurement, we identified and quantified 835 proteins with an average sequence coverage of 37.0% (Figure 1—source data 1; labeled in blue in Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The MSE mode quantified myelin proteins with a dynamic range of over four orders of magnitude parts per million (ppm).
source: The MSE mode quantified myelin proteins with a dynamic range of over four orders of magnitude parts per million (ppm), thereby allowing the reliable quantification of all myelin constituents, including the exceptionally abundant PLP, MBP, and CNP.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The UDMSE mode identified over twice as many proteins as MSE, though with a compressed dynamic range of only about three orders of magnitude ppm.
source: The UDMSE mode identified over twice as many proteins as MSE, though with a compressed dynamic range of only about three orders of magnitude ppm.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The MSE and UDMSE datasets correlated well with a correlation coefficient of >0.8.
source: Expectedly, the MSE and UDMSE datasets correlated well with a correlation coefficient of >0.8 (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 848 proteins were identified in human CNS myelin by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis.
source: Both datasets taken together, we identified 848 proteins in human CNS myelin by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Known myelin markers were enriched in the myelin fraction compared to brain homogenate.
source: When comparing the relative abundance of proteins in the myelin fraction and the corresponding homogenate, we found known myelin markers enriched in the myelin fraction (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental mass spectrometry data comparing myelin fraction to brain homogenate.

claim: Markers for other cell types or compartments were either reduced in abundance in the myelin fraction compared to brain lysate or not identified at all.
source: Markers for other cell types or compartments were either reduced in abundance in the myelin fraction compared to brain lysate or not identified at all (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental mass spectrometry data comparing myelin fraction to brain lysate.

claim: PLP accounted for 44.8% of the total myelin proteins in human white matter.
source: The most abundant myelin proteins were the structural constituents PLP, MBP, and CNP, which accounted for 44.8, 28.4, and 4.5% of the total myelin proteins, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative mass spectrometry data from the MSE dataset.

claim: MBP accounted for 28.4% of the total myelin proteins in human white matter.
source: The most abundant myelin proteins were the structural constituents PLP, MBP, and CNP, which accounted for 44.8, 28.4, and 4.5% of the total myelin proteins, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative mass spectrometry data from the MSE dataset.

claim: CNP accounted for 4.5% of the total myelin proteins in human white matter.
source: The most abundant myelin proteins were the structural constituents PLP, MBP, and CNP, which accounted for 44.8, 28.4, and 4.5% of the total myelin proteins, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative mass spectrometry data from the MSE dataset.

claim: Previously known myelin proteins constituted approximately 82% of the total human myelin protein.
source: Previously known myelin proteins constituted approximately 82% of the total human myelin protein (Figure 1d), while the remaining 18% were accounted for by other proteins, including occasional contaminants from other cellular sources (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative mass spectrometry data from the MSE dataset.

claim: The majority of known myelin proteins were identified in myelin of both humans and mice.
source: As expected, the majority of known myelin proteins were identified in myelin of both species (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative mass spectrometry data from human and mouse myelin.

claim: A subset of known myelin proteins was identified only in either human or mouse myelin.
source: However, a subset of known myelin proteins was identified only in either human or mouse myelin (Figure 2b), in agreement with the hypothesis that the protein composition of myelin is not identical across these species.
evidence: The claim is based on comparative mass spectrometry data from human and mouse myelin.

claim: PMP2 was identified in human CNS myelin.
source: For example, we noted that peripheral myelin protein 2 (PMP2, also termed P2 or fatty acid binding protein [FABP8]) was identified in human CNS myelin (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is based on mass spectrometry data from human myelin.

claim: PMP2 has long been known as a constituent of myelin in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) synthesized by Schwann cells.
source: PMP2 has long been known as a constituent of myelin in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) synthesized by Schwann cells (Greenfield et al., 1973; Uusitalo et al., 2021) but based on rodent studies was assumed to be absent from CNS myelin.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Based on rodent studies, PMP2 was assumed to be absent from CNS myelin.
source: PMP2 has long been known as a constituent of myelin in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) synthesized by Schwann cells (Greenfield et al., 1973; Uusitalo et al., 2021) but based on rodent studies was assumed to be absent from CNS myelin.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from prior rodent studies.

claim: PMP2 was readily detected in human CNS myelin by both immunoblotting and immunohistochemistry.
source: Yet, PMP2 was readily detected in human CNS myelin by both immunoblotting (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) and immunohistochemistry (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), thus confirming its mass spectrometric identification.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental immunoblotting and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: PMP2 was not detected in mouse CNS myelin by immunoblot.
source: In contrast, PMP2 was not detected in mouse CNS myelin by immunoblot (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental immunoblotting data.

claim: PMP2 was readily detected in mouse PNS myelin.
source: In agreement with prior work (Greenfield et al., 1973), PMP2 was readily detected in mouse PNS myelin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), indicating that the utilized antibodies detect PMP2 of either species.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental immunoblotting data and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Species-dependent differences exist in the protein composition of CNS myelin between humans and mice.
source: Together, this substantiates the existence of species-dependent differences in the protein composition of CNS myelin between humans and mice.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparative mass spectrometry and immunoblotting data.

claim: The human and mouse myelin proteome datasets correlated well with correlation coefficients of >0.7.
source: Indeed, the datasets correlated well with correlation coefficients of >0.7 (MSE, Figure 2c; UDMSE, Figure 2d) but clearly diverged to some extent.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of comparative mass spectrometry data.

claim: Major structural myelin proteins, including PLP, MBP, CNP, SEPTIN2, SEPTIN7, and SEPTIN8, displayed a similar relative abundance in myelin of both humans and mice.
source: We found that major structural myelin proteins, including PLP, MBP, CNP, SEPTIN2, SEPTIN7, and SEPTIN8, displayed a similar relative abundance in myelin of both species.
evidence: The claim is based on comparative mass spectrometry data from human and mouse myelin.

claim: Several myelin proteins were comparatively more abundant in human myelin, as exemplified by crystallin-αB (CRYAB), CD9, and peptidyl arginine deiminase (PADI2).
source: However, several other myelin proteins were comparatively more abundant in human myelin, as exemplified by crystallin-αB (CRYAB), CD9 (also termed tetraspanin-29 [TSPAN29]), and peptidyl arginine deiminase (PADI2), or in mouse myelin, including myelin-associated oligodendrocyte basic protein (MOBP), sirtuin-2 (SIRT2), and carbonic anhydrase 2 (CA2).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative mass spectrometry data from human and mouse myelin.

claim: Several myelin proteins were comparatively more abundant in mouse myelin, including myelin-associated oligodendrocyte basic protein (MOBP), sirtuin-2 (SIRT2), and carbonic anhydrase 2 (CA2).
source: However, several other myelin proteins were comparatively more abundant in human myelin, as exemplified by crystallin-αB (CRYAB), CD9 (also termed tetraspanin-29 [TSPAN29]), and peptidyl arginine deiminase (PADI2), or in mouse myelin, including myelin-associated oligodendrocyte basic protein (MOBP), sirtuin-2 (SIRT2), and carbonic anhydrase 2 (CA2).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative mass spectrometry data from human and mouse myelin.

claim: Immunoblotting results were generally consistent with the mass spectrometric comparison of protein abundance between human and mouse myelin.
source: Importantly, when detecting these proteins by immunoblotting in myelin of both species (Figure 2f), these results were generally consistent with the mass spectrometric comparison (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of immunoblotting and mass spectrometry data.

claim: MBP displays three main isoforms (14.0, 17.0, and 18.5 kDa) in mouse CNS myelin.
source: This is exemplified by MBP, which – owing to species-dependent alternative splicing (Campagnoni, 1988) – displays three main isoforms (14.0, 17.0, and 18.5 kDa) in mouse CNS myelin but only one dominant isoform (18.5 kDa) in human CNS myelin, in agreement with previous observations (Waehneldt and Malotka, 1980; Ishii et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MBP displays only one dominant isoform (18.5 kDa) in human CNS myelin.
source: This is exemplified by MBP, which – owing to species-dependent alternative splicing (Campagnoni, 1988) – displays three main isoforms (14.0, 17.0, and 18.5 kDa) in mouse CNS myelin but only one dominant isoform (18.5 kDa) in human CNS myelin, in agreement with previous observations (Waehneldt and Malotka, 1980; Ishii et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The protein composition of human and mouse CNS myelin is similar with respect to the relative abundance of major structural proteins but displays remarkable qualitative and quantitative differences regarding many other myelin proteins.
source: Taken together, the protein composition of human and mouse CNS myelin is similar with respect to the relative abundance of major structural proteins but displays remarkable qualitative and quantitative differences regarding many other myelin proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparative mass spectrometry and immunoblotting data.

claim: Cells from all studies distributed well across the UMAP plots in the integrated human and mouse scRNA-seq datasets.
source: Importantly, cells from all studies distributed well across the uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plots (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b), implying suitability for integration and further assessment.
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: Cells expressing markers for OPCs or MOL clustered well in both the human and mouse integrated scRNA-seq datasets.
source: Indeed, when highlighting marker gene expression on UMAPs, cells expressing markers for OPCs (CSPG4, PCDH15, PDGFRA, PTPRZ1) or MOL (ANLN, CNP, MBP, PLP1) clustered well in both the human and mouse integrated datasets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c and e).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: Multiple myelin-related transcripts displayed considerable expression only in human or mouse oligodendrocytes, as exemplified by TSPAN2, GJC3, and PMP2.
source: Notably, however, multiple myelin-related transcripts displayed considerable expression only in human or mouse oligodendrocytes, as exemplified by TSPAN2, GJC3, and PMP2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: Only 132 cells designated as NFO were comprised in the available human scRNA-seq datasets, considerably fewer compared to 10,391 NFO recovered from the mouse datasets.
source: Indeed, only 132 cells designated as NFO were comprised in the available human scRNA-seq datasets, considerably fewer compared to 10,391 NFO recovered from the mouse datasets (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative assessment of scRNA-seq datasets.

claim: Cells from both human and mouse species distributed well across the UMAPs in the integrated MOL dataset.
source: Importantly, cells from both species distributed well across the UMAPs (Figure 3b and c), providing the basis for assessing the transcriptional profiles of 41,517 human and 95,966 mouse MOL.
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: The integrated MOL dataset comprised 41,517 human and 95,966 mouse MOL.
source: Importantly, cells from both species distributed well across the UMAPs (Figure 3b and c), providing the basis for assessing the transcriptional profiles of 41,517 human and 95,966 mouse MOL.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative assessment of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: Cells expressing myelin marker transcripts (ANLN, CNP, GSN, MBP, PLLP, PLP1) distributed similarly across human and mouse MOL.
source: At the level of gene expression, cells expressing myelin marker transcripts (ANLN, CNP, GSN, MBP, PLLP, PLP1) distributed similarly across human and mouse MOL (Figure 3d), as did transcripts encoding myelination-related transcription factors (MYRF, SOX10) (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: Transcripts encoding myelination-related transcription factors (MYRF, SOX10) distributed similarly across human and mouse MOL.
source: At the level of gene expression, cells expressing myelin marker transcripts (ANLN, CNP, GSN, MBP, PLLP, PLP1) distributed similarly across human and mouse MOL (Figure 3d), as did transcripts encoding myelination-related transcription factors (MYRF, SOX10) (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: Multiple myelin-related transcripts displayed exclusive or predominant expression in MOL of only one of the species, as exemplified by PMP2, PADI2, CA2, TSPAN2, and GJC3.
source: Notably, multiple myelin-related transcripts displayed exclusive or predominant expression in MOL of only one of the species, as exemplified by PMP2, PADI2, CA2, TSPAN2, and GJC3 (Figure 3f).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: The averaged vdW-normalized mRNA-abundance profiles of all 3000 integration features correlated with a coefficient of 0.59 between human and mouse MOL.
source: When comparing all 3000 integration features, the averaged vdW-normalized mRNA-abundance profiles correlated reasonably well with a coefficient of 0.59 (gray data points in Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: A comparatively higher correlation coefficient of 0.84 was found when comparing only known myelin-related transcripts between human and mouse MOL.
source: However, a comparatively higher correlation coefficient of 0.84 was found when comparing only known myelin-related transcripts (n = 37 transcripts; highlighted as blue data points in Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: The transcriptional profiles of known myelin-related transcripts are more similar between humans and mice than those of the other transcripts expressed in MOL.
source: This implies that the transcriptional profiles of known myelin-related transcripts are more similar between humans and mice than those of the other transcripts expressed in MOL.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from statistical analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: The abundance of several transcripts encoding structural myelin proteins, including PLP1, MBP, and CNP, was essentially equal between human and mouse MOL.
source: In particular, the abundance of several transcripts encoding structural myelin proteins, including PLP1, MBP, and CNP, was essentially equal between human and mouse MOL.
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: The abundance of transcripts for myelin-related transcription factors (MYRF, OLIG1, OLIG2, SOX10) was roughly similar between human and mouse MOL.
source: In similarity, the abundance of transcripts for myelin-related transcription factors (MYRF, OLIG1, OLIG2, SOX10) was also roughly similar (labeled in green in Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: The abundance of the Mal-transcript encoding myelin and lymphocyte protein (MAL) correlates well between human and mouse MOL.
source: As an example, the abundance of the Mal-transcript encoding myelin and lymphocyte protein (MAL) correlates well between human and mouse MOL (labeled in orange Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: MAL is a known myelin protein which is not identified by mass spectrometry because of its nonsuitable tryptic digest pattern.
source: MAL is a known myelin protein (Schaeren-Wiemers et al., 2004), which, however, is not identified by mass spectrometry because of its nonsuitable tryptic digest pattern.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about MAL and supported by citation.

claim: The integrated scRNA-seq profiles of MOL generally correlated well between humans and mice, particularly with respect to known myelin-related mRNAs.
source: Together, the integrated scRNA-seq profiles of MOL generally correlated well between humans and mice, particularly with respect to known myelin-related mRNAs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: Several transcripts displayed a qualitatively or quantitatively divergent abundance when compared between human and mouse MOL.
source: However, several transcripts displayed a qualitatively or quantitatively divergent abundance when compared between the species (Figure 3f, Figure 3—figure supplement 1f, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: Correlation coefficients of <0.5 were calculated when comparing the myelin proteome datasets with the averaged vdW-normalized mRNA abundance profile of MOL in the respective same species.
source: Next, we compared our human (Figure 1—source data 1) and mouse myelin (Jahn et al., 2020) proteome datasets (by MSE or UDMSE) with the averaged vdW-normalized mRNA abundance profile of MOL in the respective same species. We calculated correlation coefficients of <0.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis comparing proteome and transcriptome data.

claim: The degree of correlation between the myelin proteome and the MOL transcriptome within the same species is considerably lower than that between the myelin proteome or the MOL transcriptome, respectively, across the two species.
source: The degree of correlation between the myelin proteome and the MOL transcriptome within the same species is thus considerably lower than that between the myelin proteome (Figure 2c and d) or the MOL transcriptome (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), respectively, across the two species.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from statistical analysis comparing proteome and transcriptome data.

claim: KNN clustering identified five potential subpopulations of MOL in the integrated human and mouse scRNA-seq dataset.
source: Indeed, k-nearest neighbor (KNN) clustering identified five potential subpopulations of MOL (labeled as clusters 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 in Figure 4a–c).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic clustering analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: All MOL subpopulations displayed approximately similar expression levels of marker genes encoding structural myelin proteins (PLP1, MBP, CNP, CLDN11, MAG).
source: Notably, all subpopulations displayed approximately similar expression levels of marker genes encoding structural myelin proteins (PLP1, MBP, CNP, CLDN11, MAG) (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: The MOL subpopulations were defined by varying degrees of expression of other transcripts, including CD9 and OPALIN (cluster 0), APOD, KLK6, and S100B (cluster 1), APOE and CST3 (cluster 2), CA2 and PTGS (cluster 3), and SIRT2 and NFASC (cluster 4).
source: However, the subpopulations were defined by varying degrees of expression of other transcripts, including the myelin-related CD9 and OPALIN (cluster 0), APOD, KLK6, and S100B (cluster 1), APOE and CST3 (cluster 2), CA2 and PTGS (cluster 3), and SIRT2 and NFASC (cluster 4) (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: Both human and mouse MOL comprise all five subpopulations to an approximately similar extent.
source: Less speculatively, both human and mouse MOL comprise all five subpopulations to an approximately similar extent (Figure 4c), implying that none of these MOL subpopulations is restricted to either one of these species.
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: None of the MOL subpopulations is restricted to either humans or mice.
source: Less speculatively, both human and mouse MOL comprise all five subpopulations to an approximately similar extent (Figure 4c), implying that none of these MOL subpopulations is restricted to either one of these species.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from bioinformatic analysis of integrated scRNA-seq data.

claim: The septin subunits SEPTIN2, SEPTIN4, SEPTIN7, and SEPTIN8 displayed a molar stoichiometry of about 1:1:2:2 in human CNS myelin.
source: For example, the filament-forming septins SEPTIN2, SEPTIN4, SEPTIN7, and SEPTIN8 displayed a molar stoichiometry of about 1:1:2:2 in human CNS myelin.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative mass spectrometry data from human myelin.

claim: The same septin subunits are comprised in myelin of mice with a similar molar stoichiometry.
source: Notably, the same septin subunits are also comprised in myelin of mice with a similar molar stoichiometry (Jahn et al., 2020), a likely prerequisite for their assembly into similar core multimers and higher-order structures.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative mass spectrometry data from mouse myelin and supported by citation.

claim: These septin subunits assemble into membrane-associated filaments that stabilize the adaxonal compartment of CNS myelin.
source: Indeed, experiments in mice have previously shown that these septin subunits assemble into membrane-associated filaments that stabilize the adaxonal compartment of CNS myelin (Patzig et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work in mice.

claim: The predominant core multimer of septins in myelin is a hexamer of septins 2/4-8-7-7-8-2/4.
source: Integrating the current view on septin assembly (Soroor et al., 2021) and the relative abundance of septin subunits in myelin, it is possible to deduce that the predominant core multimer in myelin is a hexamer of septins 2/4-8-7-7-8-2/4.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from integrating established knowledge about septin assembly with quantitative proteomics data.

claim: The comparatively low abundance of SEPTIN9 in myelin implies that core octamers occur less frequently.
source: The comparatively low abundance of SEPTIN9 in myelin implies that core octamers occur less frequently.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from quantitative proteomics data.

claim: For each septin core hexamer, up to one molecule of the adaptor protein anillin is present in CNS myelin.
source: Assessing the relative abundance of myelin proteins also allows deducing that for each core hexamer up to one molecule of the adaptor protein anillin that facilitates septin assembly (Erwig et al., 2019b) is present in CNS myelin.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from quantitative proteomics data and supported by citation.

claim: The relative abundance and multimer composition of myelin septins are conserved between human and mouse CNS myelin.
source: Together, the relative abundance and multimer composition of myelin septins emerge as conserved between human and mouse CNS myelin, similar to that of other structural myelin proteins, including PLP, MBP and CNP.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparative quantitative proteomics data.

claim: TSPAN2 was previously established as a myelin protein in mice and rats.
source: For example, the tetraspan-transmembrane proteins TSPAN2 (Birling et al., 1999; Terada et al., 2002; de Monasterio-Schrader et al., 2013) and GPM6B/M6B/Rhombex29 (Shimokawa and Miura, 2000; Werner et al., 2013) were previously established as myelin proteins in mice and rats, and they were readily identified in CNS myelin of mice by both mass spectrometry (Jahn et al., 2020) and immunoblot.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GPM6B was previously established as a myelin protein in mice and rats.
source: For example, the tetraspan-transmembrane proteins TSPAN2 (Birling et al., 1999; Terada et al., 2002; de Monasterio-Schrader et al., 2013) and GPM6B/M6B/Rhombex29 (Shimokawa and Miura, 2000; Werner et al., 2013) were previously established as myelin proteins in mice and rats, and they were readily identified in CNS myelin of mice by both mass spectrometry (Jahn et al., 2020) and immunoblot.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TSPAN2 and GPM6B were readily identified in CNS myelin of mice by both mass spectrometry and immunoblot.
source: For example, the tetraspan-transmembrane proteins TSPAN2 (Birling et al., 1999; Terada et al., 2002; de Monasterio-Schrader et al., 2013) and GPM6B/M6B/Rhombex29 (Shimokawa and Miura, 2000; Werner et al., 2013) were previously established as myelin proteins in mice and rats, and they were readily identified in CNS myelin of mice by both mass spectrometry (Jahn et al., 2020) and immunoblot.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data and supported by citation.

claim: TSPAN2 and GPM6B were of very low abundance or virtually undetectable in human myelin by both mass spectrometry and immunoblot.
source: However, these proteins were of very low abundance or virtually undetectable in human myelin by both techniques.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental mass spectrometry and immunoblotting data.

claim: TSPAN2 contributes to immunomodulation in experimental mice.
source: It has been established in experimental mice that TSPAN2 and GPM6B contribute to immunomodulation (de Monasterio-Schrader et al., 2013) and myelin biogenesis (Werner et al., 2013), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work in mice.

claim: GPM6B contributes to myelin biogenesis in experimental mice.
source: It has been established in experimental mice that TSPAN2 and GPM6B contribute to immunomodulation (de Monasterio-Schrader et al., 2013) and myelin biogenesis (Werner et al., 2013), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work in mice.

claim: The mouse and human orthologs of TSPAN2 and GPM6B do not contribute equally to their respective functions.
source: The present data thus imply that the mouse and human orthologs do not contribute equally to these functions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparative proteomics data showing differential abundance.

claim: GJC3 has been established as a myelin protein in mice and rats.
source: The gap junction protein GJC3/CX29 has also been established as a myelin protein in mice and rats and is thought to mediate intercellular coupling via gap junctions (Nagy et al., 2003; Kleopa et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GJC3 is thought to mediate intercellular coupling via gap junctions.
source: The gap junction protein GJC3/CX29 has also been established as a myelin protein in mice and rats and is thought to mediate intercellular coupling via gap junctions (Nagy et al., 2003; Kleopa et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents a hypothesis.

claim: GJC3 has been readily identified mass spectrometrically and by immunoblotting in mouse but not human myelin.
source: Similar to TSPAN2 and GPM6B, GJC3 has been readily identified mass spectrometrically and by immunoblotting in mouse but not human myelin.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental mass spectrometry and immunoblotting data.

claim: Deletion of the Gjc3-gene in mice did not have evident morphological or functional consequences for CNS myelin or oligodendrocytes.
source: Interestingly, though, deletion of the Gjc3-gene in mice did not have evident morphological or functional consequences for CNS myelin or oligodendrocytes (Altevogt and Paul, 2004; Eiberger et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work in mice.

claim: The benefit for mouse CNS myelin to comprise GJC3 remains unknown.
source: The benefit for mouse CNS myelin to comprise GJC3 thus remains unknown at this time.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the lack of evident phenotype in Gjc3-deficient mice.

claim: PMP2 is a membrane-phosphoinositide-binding protein.
source: On the other hand, PMP2 (previously termed P2 or FABP8), a membrane-phosphoinositide-binding protein (Abe et al., 2021), has long been known as a constituent of peripheral myelin generated by Schwann cells in the PNS (Uusitalo et al., 2021; Brostoff et al., 1975; Kitamura et al., 1980) and actually considered a marker to discriminate peripheral from central myelin (Franz et al., 1981; DeArmond et al., 1980; Whitaker, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PMP2 has long been known as a constituent of peripheral myelin generated by Schwann cells in the PNS.
source: On the other hand, PMP2 (previously termed P2 or FABP8), a membrane-phosphoinositide-binding protein (Abe et al., 2021), has long been known as a constituent of peripheral myelin generated by Schwann cells in the PNS (Uusitalo et al., 2021; Brostoff et al., 1975; Kitamura et al., 1980) and actually considered a marker to discriminate peripheral from central myelin (Franz et al., 1981; DeArmond et al., 1980; Whitaker, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PMP2 was considered a marker to discriminate peripheral from central myelin.
source: On the other hand, PMP2 (previously termed P2 or FABP8), a membrane-phosphoinositide-binding protein (Abe et al., 2021), has long been known as a constituent of peripheral myelin generated by Schwann cells in the PNS (Uusitalo et al., 2021; Brostoff et al., 1975; Kitamura et al., 1980) and actually considered a marker to discriminate peripheral from central myelin (Franz et al., 1981; DeArmond et al., 1980; Whitaker, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The experiments establishing PMP2 as a marker to discriminate peripheral from central myelin involved bovine and rodent but not human samples.
source: Notably, the experiments establishing this view involved bovine and rodent but not human samples.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the cited literature.

claim: The PNS of Pmp2-deficient mice displayed an altered myelin lipid profile associated with reduced motor nerve conduction velocity.
source: A lead may come from the investigation of the PNS of Pmp2-deficient mice, which displayed an altered myelin lipid profile associated with reduced motor nerve conduction velocity (Zenker et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work in mice.
